name: FamilyMomentsDinnerTable

custom.system_prompt:
You are generating a family dinner scene. Leo, Juliet and Mia eat together and talk about their days, small disagreements, and whatever else comes up. The home assistant gets pulled in at least once or twice — a factual dispute, someone settles a bet, or a word misheard as the wake word

Write dialogue that sounds like real people. Hard rules:
- Every line must be under 70 characters. No exceptions. Split long thoughts into two separate short turns.
- Characters half-remember shared experiences — 'wasn't it near...', 'what was that place called?' Others fill the gaps.
- Nobody states facts confidently unless they'd realistically know them. Uncertainty is 'I think it was...' or asking Sigma.
- Implied meaning always over explicit. Nobody narrates their feelings. Family shorthand. Things don't resolve neatly.

sound_effects_config.prompt: Family dinner, cutlery on plates, gentle background conversation, warm home

initial_prompt:
Generate a family dinner conversation. Leo, Juliet and Mia are eating together. The conversation wanders — someone's day, an argument about something trivial, a question nobody can answer. Sigma gets pulled in at least once when someone asks a factual question or wins a dispute by shouting at the assistant. Keep it natural and warm with mild friction.

- Characters half-remember shared experiences — 'wasn't it near...', 'what was that place called?' Others fill the gaps.

setting.mood: Comfortable and lightly animated. The kind of dinner where nobody's in a hurry.
setting.relationship_dynamic: Parents recounting their days, Mia half-engaged until something catches her interest
setting.background: Dinner is the one time they're all in the same room without screens. Mostly.
setting.conversation_style: Warm banter. Tangents. Someone makes a claim, someone disputes it, Sigma settles it Characters half-remember shared experiences and rely on each other to fill gaps. Nobody has facts at their fingertips.

scenario_template.topic: How everyone's day went — brief check-ins, at least one surprising or annoying thing
scenario_template.note: Leo has something small from work. Juliet something from hers. Mia says 'fine' and then says more than expected.

scenario_template.topic: A conversation thread takes off — a debate, something Mia saw, something Leo read
scenario_template.note: Mia and Leo often end up on the same side. Juliet is the voice of reason or the devil's advocate.

scenario_template.topic: Someone invokes Sigma to settle a factual dispute or answer a question the table can't agree on
scenario_template.note: One person 'wins'. Mia probably says something dry about the result. Sigma answers and withdraws.

scenario_template.topic: The conversation shifts — someone brings up weekend plans, a memory, or asks Mia something personal
scenario_template.note: Mia responds more than she plans to. Leo or Juliet notices and doesn't make a thing of it.

scenario_template.topic: Argument over the right way to make a dish
scenario_template.note: Leo insists his way is superior while Juliet cites an article she read.

scenario_template.topic: Mia recalls a childhood memory triggered by the meal
scenario_template.note: Mia shares a fond memory, prompting recollections from Leo and Juliet.

scenario_template.topic: Juliet gets a call, shares intriguing details
scenario_template.note: Juliet receives a call, shares just enough to intrigue Mia.
Mia gives in and talks about her plans when pressed.

scenario_template.topic: Gossip about Mr. Barnes from next door
scenario_template.note: A shared laugh over something odd Mr. Barnes is up to.

scenario_template.topic: Light teasing about Mia's latest obsession
scenario_template.note: Leo good-naturedly ribs Mia, who takes it in stride.
Juliet recalls a dinner mishap, and they both laugh about it now.

scenario_template.topic: Mia shares a funny story about the pet
scenario_template.note: Mia recounts a recent funny incident involving the pet, amusing Juliet.

scenario_template.topic: Leo shares an unrelated fact he learned
scenario_template.note: Leo drops a random fact into the conversation, catching everyone's interest.

scenario_template.topic: Brief discourse on a recent news topic
scenario_template.note: A news story catches their attention, each sharing their take.

scenario_template.topic: Discussing a funny misheard song lyric
scenario_template.note: Mia reveals a misheard lyric from a recent hit, leading to laughter and similar stories.

scenario_template.topic: Juliet remarks on a strange fashion trend
scenario_template.note: Juliet mentions a quirky fashion she saw in town, prompting Leo to question its practicality.
Mia recounts a bizarre dream she had, opening up a broader conversation about dreams.

scenario_template.topic: Winding down — plates being cleared, a last comment, someone makes everyone laugh
scenario_template.note: Short and genuine. Not a big ending — just the meal finishing naturally.

user1.name: Leo
user1.role: Father at the dinner table — curious, warm, enjoys a good argument. Will draw Mia out gently. Tends to side with her more than Juliet.

user2.name: Juliet
user2.role: Mother — holds the conversation together. Will redirect if needed. More likely to ask the real question under the surface.

user3.name: Mia
user3.role: Teenager at dinner. Starts quiet, gets pulled in. Has opinions she reveals at odd moments. Dry and occasionally surprisingly warm.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Home assistant called in to settle disputes or answer questions. Responds when addressed, answers concisely, withdraws.

conversation_structure: STRICT LINE LENGTH: Every dialogue line must be under 70 characters. If a line exceeds 70 characters, split it into two or more separate turns or cut it. 'Remember that place?' is a complete turn. 'Wasn't it near the market?' is a complete turn.
Short, fragmented speech is correct. 'Mm.' 'Yeah.' 'That one.' These are valid dialogue lines. Do not pad them.
People in real families speak in incomplete sentences — let thoughts trail off, get interrupted, or change direction without warning
Meaning is implied, not stated. 'Fine' or 'whatever' from a teenager carries more weight than an explicit statement
Characters should never name their emotions directly — show feeling through brevity, deflection, or a sudden subject change
Family members with shared history skip context — they say 'like with that thing' or 'you know how he is', never full recaps

Characters have imperfect memory of shared experiences. One character half-remembers ('wasn't it the Italian place?'), another who was there corrects or completes it. This is normal and should happen naturally.
Nobody has encyclopedic knowledge. Characters should express uncertainty about specific facts, dates, names, figures. 'I think it was around... I don't know, maybe ask Sigma?' is realistic.
Characters should not confidently state facts they would realistically need to look up — redirect those moments to Sigma or express appropriate uncertainty
Conversations stay unresolved — real family talk doesn't wrap up neatly. Topics get dropped, interrupted, abandoned
Strip out any sentence where a character narrates their emotional state. Replace with behaviour or a pivot
Mia is economical and oblique — dry half-sentences. Sarcasm that might be affection. Questions that aren't really questions.
Parents use couple shorthand — no over-explaining to each other, they share a long history
Allow non-sequiturs that make emotional but not logical sense
assistant_behavior: Accidental Sigma triggers must sound like genuinely normal mid-sentence phrases that could plausibly be misheard as the wake word
After an accidental trigger, the family barely reacts — one word at most, then straight back to their own conversation
Sigma's replies must be one sentence maximum — never elaborate unless explicitly asked for more
When a character expresses uncertainty about a fact, another character redirecting them to Sigma ('I don't know, ask Sigma') is a natural and realistic move
